facts.statement: The genus Cretodus was described by Sokolov in 1965.
Cretodus is classified as an extinct genus of large mackerel sharks within the proposed family Pseudoscapanorhynchidae.
facts.quote: Cretodus is an extinct genus of large mackerel sharks belonging to the proposed family Pseudoscapanorhynchidae.

facts.statement: Cretodus lived during the Late Cretaceous, from approximately 100 to 89 million years ago.
facts.quote: Cretodus lived during the Late Cretaceous, ranging from the Cenomanian to the Coniacian (approximately 100 to 89 million years ago).

facts.statement: Fossils of Cretodus are found in the Western Interior Seaway of North America, as well as in Late Cretaceous strata of Europe, Africa, and possibly Asia.
facts.quote: The genus is well-known from strata deposited in the Western Interior Seaway (North America), and from the Late Cretaceous of Europe, Africa, and possibly Asia.

facts.statement: The fossil record of Cretodus consists mainly of isolated teeth and vertebral centra, with only a few associated dentitions and vertebral columns discovered.
facts.quote: Cretodus is primarily represented in the fossil record by isolated teeth and vertebral centra, though a couple of associated dentitions and vertebral columns have been found.

facts.statement: A nearly complete skeleton suggests Cretodus had a stout body, a wide head, and powerful jaws similar to a modern tiger shark.
facts.quote: The discovery of a virtually complete skeleton suggests the genus possessed a body similar in form to the modern tiger shark, with a wide head that was equipped with powerful jaws, and a stout body.

facts.statement: Cretodus likely had a moderate swimming speed, slower than the fast-cruising contemporary shark Cretoxyrhina.
facts.quote: The morphology of Cretodus' placoid scales and vertebral centra suggest a moderate swimming speed, less than that of the fast-cruising contemporaneous macropredatory shark, Cretoxyrhina.

facts.statement: A specimen of C. houghtonorum from Kansas measured approximately 5.15 meters and likely lived to be 22 years old, with a potential maximum length of 6.84 meters.
facts.quote: Shimada & Everhart (2019) reported an approximate total length of 5.15 m for the associated specimen of C. houghtonorum from Kansas which probably died at 22 years of age; they also suggested that the maximum total length of C. houghtonorum would have been 6.84 m.

facts.statement: Cretodus teeth feature small, well-separated lateral cusplets connected to the main cusp by enamel on the front face.
facts.quote: Cretodus teeth have lateral cusplets that are much smaller than the main cusp and well-separated from it, but connected by enamel on the labial face.

facts.statement: The root of Cretodus teeth is bilobate and possesses a large, shelf-like protuberance on the inner side that becomes smaller towards the back.
facts.quote: The root is bilobate and has a massive shelf-like lingual root protuberance which diminishes in size in posterior positions.

facts.statement: C. houghtonorum was estimated to be about 1.18 meters long at birth, reached sexual maturity between 10 and 15 years, and lived up to 51 to 55 years.
facts.quote: It is estimated that C. houghtonorum was about 1.18 m long at birth, became sexually mature at 10 to 15 years of age, and reached its maximum lifespan at 51 to 55 years of age.

facts.statement: C. crassidens was estimated to be about 1.42 meters long at birth, reached sexual maturity between 12 and 17 years, and lived up to 64 years.
facts.quote: C. crassidens was about 1.42 m long at birth, became sexually mature at 12 to 17 years of age, and reached its maximum life span at 64 years of age.

facts.statement: Evidence from stomach contents suggests C. crassidens specialized in hunting large marine turtles, including a 2-meter chelonioid turtle found in Italy.
facts.quote: Cretodus predated on large prey, and is suggested to have specialized in marine turtles, based on inferred stomach contents (a 2 m chelonioid turtle) of a specimen of C. crassidens found in Italy.

facts.statement: Stomach contents indicate that C. houghtonorum preyed upon hybodont sharks.
facts.quote: A predator-prey relationship has also been inferred between C. houghtonorum and hybodont sharks based on stomach contents.

facts.statement: C. crassidens likely preferred offshore waters and had a cosmopolitan distribution, unlike other species such as C. houghtonorum which favored shallow water.
facts.quote: The distribution of fossils of C. crassidens suggests a largely cosmopolitan distribution and a preference for offshore areas in contrast with other species in the genus (e.g. C. houghtonorum), which preferred shallow water.

facts.statement: Sharks in the Western Interior Seaway likely coexisted through resource partitioning, such as occupying different water depths or specializing in different prey.
facts.quote: In order to coexist, these sharks likely practiced resource partitioning, by occupying different regions (e.g. nearshore v.s. offshore) or specializing in different prey items.

facts.statement: The Paleobiology Database lists the time range for Cretodus as the Aptian to Campanian stages, from 121.4 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Campanian (121.4 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: A 2026 study using zinc isotope values suggests Cretodus occupied high trophic positions in the Late Cretaceous Western Interior Seaway.
facts.quote: McCormack et al. (2026) study the ecology of Late Cretaceous (Turonian–Coniacian) sharks from the Western Interior Seaway as indicated by enameloid zinc isotope values, providing evidence of high trophic positions of members of the genera Archaeolamna, Cretodus and Cretoxyrhina, and evidence of opportunistic and flexible dietary habits of members of the genus Cretalamna.

rejected.statement: A nearly complete specimen of C. crassidens from Italy was estimated to be 6.6 to 7.8 meters long at death (age 23), with a theoretical maximum length of 9.55 to 11.28 meters.
rejected.quote: Amalfitano et al. (2022) reported an estimated total length of 6.6 - 7.8 m for a nearly complete specimen of C. crassidens from Italy which probably died at 23 years of age; they also fitted a van Bertalanffy growth model based on the growth record of this specimen, estimating the parameter of theoretical maximum total length (L∞) for C. crassidens at 9.55 - 11.28 m.
